claims.text: The starting catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy with homogeneously distributed base metals and a low, non-optimized platinum-group-metal content.
Mild acid leaching will preferentially remove the more labile elements from the starting alloy.
A short anneal at approximately 150 °C in H2 will stabilize atomically dispersed Pt sites on the dealloyed surface.
The combined dealloying and annealing treatment will form single-atom Pt sites embedded in the high-entropy alloy matrix.
High-entropy-alloyed single-atom Pt sites can act synergistically with surrounding non-noble elements to govern oxidation-reaction kinetics.
Atomically dispersed Pt sites have high intrinsic activity for low-temperature automotive CO and hydrocarbon oxidation.
The isolated nature of the Pt sites makes them less prone to H2O poisoning.
The isolated nature of the Pt sites makes them less prone to NO poisoning.
The high-entropy matrix thermodynamically stabilizes Pt species against coarsening and sintering.
The dealloyed catalyst will have a lower CO and hydrocarbon light-off temperature than the untreated catalyst and will enable efficient oxidation below 150 °C.
The dealloyed catalyst will tolerate H2O and NO better than the untreated catalyst.
The dealloyed catalyst will retain more activity and a more stable morphology after accelerated thermal aging than the untreated catalyst.
A high-entropy single-atom Pt architecture can provide activity and durability while using a low Pt loading.
The claimed improvements will apply during transient low-temperature exhaust exposure containing H2O and NO and after thermal cycling intended to mimic long-term mileage.
Annealing at approximately 150 °C in H2 replicates conditions below typical automotive exhaust temperatures during transient operation.
Overly harsh or overly mild dealloying can respectively damage matrix integrity or fail to optimize Pt dispersion.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in light-off, poison tolerance, and post-aging activity relative to the untreated control would falsify the combined-performance hypothesis.
